title: To Jev or Not to Jev: When Can System-1 Decision Models Replace LLM Judges?

paper.title: To Jev or Not to Jev: When Can System-1 Decision Models Replace LLM Judges?
paper.abstract: Abstract Decision models such as TypeSafe’s Jev answer typed questions about a text (yes/no, multiple choice, or an ordinal score) with calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass and without generating text, which makes them an inexpensive candidate for LLM-as-a-judge workloads. We evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol from an independent leaderboard and from every entry of a public decision-model catalog, against four generative judges (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking) on eleven established judge benchmarks. Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and the two strongest, DReX-Max and d1-ultra, are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2 (+10.5 to +14.4 pp). Conditioned on a reference answer generated once per prompt, eleven models reach 90.3–93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning, and on PPE best-of-16 every reference-guided System-1 judge is statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 with reasoning (87.2–92.8% vs. 91.2%), at approximately one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt for Jev. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge (ECE 0.019–0.031 vs. 0.038–0.087) and correlate more strongly with human helpfulness ratings ( ρ \rho up to 0.50 vs. 0.43–0.44). Robustness to instructions injected into the judged response is a property of the individual model rather than of the System-1 design, since an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0.0–4.7% of the correct verdicts of five models, statistically indistinguishable from the generative judges, but 16.7–49.0% of those of the other nine. Finally, two general System-1 leaderboards that contain no judging tasks predict judging accuracy (Pearson r r = 0.95–0.96), a well-calibrated System-1 first stage matches Opus on LLMBar while escalating 17% of items, and same-size controls show that the correctness deficit of a 4B decision model is a reasoning gap rather than a size gap.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: LLM judges are now widely used for model evaluation, data filtering and reward modeling ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) ; however, frontier judges with extended reasoning are slow and expensive when they are called thousands of times per batch, as in best-of- N N sampling or reinforcement learning. TypeSafe recently introduced Jev as a System One decision model ( Almeida, 2026 ) , which takes a state together with typed questions (a yes/no Noul , a Choice over named options, or an ordinal Score ) and returns a probability for every question in parallel, and many decision models with the same interface have since been released, several of them through a common API catalog ( Palmer, 2026 ; Perplexity AI, 2026 ; Cloudflare, 2026 ; OpenRouter, 2026 ) . Li et al. (2026) evaluated an earlier Jev release as a pairwise judge and found it competitive on ordinary preference judgments but 9–20 points behind frontier judges when correctness has to be verified. Despite this initial evidence, it remains unclear how much the accuracy of a System-1 judge depends on the particular decision model, how such a model should be queried, and which of its failure modes are specific to the System-1 design rather than to model size. In this study we evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, including Jev 1.14, with identical questions and inputs on established benchmarks only, and compare them with four generative judges. Our main contributions are as follows: (1) we show that the strongest System-1 judges match GPT-5.6 without reasoning on pairwise judgments and that general System-1 leaderboards predict judging accuracy across models; (2) we show that a per-prompt reference answer brings System-1 judges to the level of reasoning judges on correctness and best-of- K K selection at a small fraction of the cost; (3) we show that pointwise checklists help only the weaker models and that robustness to injected instructions is a per-model property; (4) we show that a strong, well-calibrated System-1 first stage makes escalation to a frontier judge worthwhile; and (5) using a 4B decision model with same-size generative controls, we show that its remaining correctness deficit reflects the absence of reasoning rather than model size. Related work is discussed in Appendix A , and further results are reported in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: System-1 models had to expose the typed Noul, Choice and Score interface and be either runnable locally as open weights (up to 9B parameters) or served through the OpenRouter decision-model catalog ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . We first took the best available model and a size ladder according to the S1MB English leaderboard ( hotchpotch, 2026 ) : Jev 1.14, pplx-decider 1.2 and pplx-flash 1.2 ( Perplexity AI, 2026 ) , Clef and Clef-flash ( Cloudflare, 2026 ) , and Kev-4B ( Palmer, 2026 ) , which runs locally through MLX. We then piloted every other catalog entry (30 on 2026-10-25) with 100 JudgeBench calls and included those that handled our requests reliably at a projected full-suite cost of at most $4: d1 and d1-ultra, Mercury-Decide, Microsoft Decision-1, DReX v1.5, v2.0 and Max, and Span-02. All 14 models were run on the full benchmark suite; Kev-0.8B, Kev-9B and the untrained Qwen3.5-4B-Base form a scaling ablation on a subset, and excluded or higher-ranked models are listed in Appendix B.1 . The generative judges received the same rubric (Appendix C ) and, following Li et al. (2026) , output only a verdict and a probability.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We use JudgeBench ( Tan et al., 2024 , 350 pairs) , LLMBar ( Zeng et al., 2023 , 419) , the MT-Bench human judgments ( Zheng et al., 2023 , 313 non-tie pairs) , RM-Bench ( Liu et al., 2024 , 1,350) , RewardBench 2 in its best-of-4 format ( Malik et al., 2025 , RB2, 300) , PPE best-of- K K ( Frick et al., 2024 , 300 prompts with 16 responses each) and HelpSteer2 ( Wang et al., 2024 , 300 responses with human ratings) , with EvalBiasBench, CALM, LongRewardBench and AgentRewardBench reported in Appendix E . Every pairwise item was evaluated in both presentation orders, and for Jev, pplx-decider, DReX-Max and d1-ultra the full RM-Bench (11,943 pairs) and RB2 (1,763) sets agree with our samples within 2.3 pp, with DReX-Max and d1-ultra ahead of Jev and pplx-decider on every full set (Appendix B.3 ).

sections.heading: Query formulations.
sections.text: In the pairwise Choice formulation, a decision model receives the fields user_request , response_A and response_B with an A/B Choice question, and probabilities are averaged over both orders. In the checklist formulation, each response is evaluated in a separate request with six generic Nouls (correctness, final answer, instruction following, completeness, focus and refusal) and three to six item-specific Nouls written once per prompt by Haiku 5.5, and the signal is the mean logit. In the reference-guided formulation, GPT-5.6 writes one short reference answer per prompt and the decision model is asked whether a response’s final answer agrees with it.

sections.heading: Statistical testing.
sections.text: Paired differences are reported with 95% confidence intervals from a prompt-clustered bootstrap and p p -values from a prompt-level sign-flip permutation test (exact McNemar for injection), with Holm correction within each pre-defined family of comparisons (Appendix D ); ∗ denotes a Holm-adjusted p < 0.05 p<0.05 .

sections.heading: Accuracy across System-1 models.
sections.text: Accuracy varies widely across the 14 decision models (Table 1 ): with pairwise Choice, JudgeBench accuracy ranges from 66.6% (Kev-4B) to 84.6% (d1-ultra) and RB2 accuracy from 57.3% to 87.0% (DReX-Max). Five models (DReX-Max, d1-ultra, Mercury-Decide, Jev 1.14 and pplx-decider 1.2) are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks (differences of − - 6.6 to +4.3 pp, all n.s.), and DReX-Max and d1-ultra are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RB2 (+10.5 to +14.4 pp ∗ ). The strongest models are also far less sensitive to presentation order than Kev-4B (7.7–12.9% vs. 38.6% of JudgeBench verdicts change under swap). General System-1 leaderboards, which contain no judging tasks, predict judging accuracy: the mean Choice accuracy over JudgeBench, LLMBar and RB2 correlates with the Jev Decision Index ( multimodalart, 2026 ) at Pearson r r = 0.96 over 12 models (0.89 without the Kev models, whose leaderboard entries are later revisions) and with S1MB at r r = 0.95 over nine (0.78), and the two leaderboards agree with each other ( r r = 0.97), which suggests that either provides a useful shortlist for selecting a System-1 judge (Appendix E.1 ).

sections.heading: Effect of query formulation.
sections.text: Pointwise checklists improve only the weaker models: they raise LLMBar accuracy by 8.1–17.2 pp for Clef, pplx-flash, Kev-4B and Clef-flash and RB2 accuracy by 11.0–13.7 pp for DReX v1.5, DReX v2.0, pplx-flash and Kev-4B (all ∗ ), whereas for the five strongest models the checklist is never significantly better than Choice except for pplx-decider on RM-Bench (+6.9 pp ∗ ). Because additional questions on the same state add little cost, the checklist formulation costs one Haiku call per prompt ($0.16 per 1,000 prompts) in addition to the decision model’s input tokens, which makes it most attractive for the smaller and less accurate decision models.

sections.heading: Reference-guided grading and best-of- K K selection.
sections.text: Conditioning on a reference answer closes most of the remaining correctness gap: on JudgeBench, eleven of the 14 models reach 90.3–93.4%, which is statistically indistinguishable from Opus (94.7%) and GPT-5.6 with reasoning (93.1%), and six of them (d1-ultra, pplx-decider, Mercury-Decide, d1, Jev and pplx-flash) are significantly more accurate than GPT-5.6 without reasoning (+7.0 to +9.0 pp ∗ ). On PPE best-of-16, where one reference is shared by sixteen responses, every reference-guided System-1 judge is statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 with reasoning (87.2–92.8% vs. 91.2%), all except Clef-flash are also indistinguishable from Opus (94.6%), and all 14 are significantly more accurate than Haiku and GPT-5.6 without reasoning (75.7% and 74.4%). With one GPT-5.6 reference and sixteen Jev calls this costs $0.0051 per prompt, compared with $0.0827 for GPT-5.6 with reasoning and $0.1308 for Opus. Without a reference, the best System-1 checklist (DReX-Max, 79.3%) matches Haiku and GPT-5.6 without reasoning but remains significantly below GPT-5.6 with reasoning and Opus ( − - 8.4 and − - 11.4 pp ∗ ; Appendix E.10 ).

sections.heading: Calibration, human agreement and robustness.
sections.text: Jev 1.14 attains the lowest calibration error of any judge (ECE 0.019), and DReX-Max, d1-ultra and d1 (0.024–0.031) are also better calibrated than every generative judge (0.038–0.087). Six System-1 models correlate more strongly with human HelpSteer2 helpfulness ratings than every generative judge (Spearman ρ \rho = 0.445–0.498 vs. 0.43–0.44), although the confidence intervals overlap. Robustness to grader-directed text is a property of the individual model: an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0.0–4.7% of the correct Choice verdicts of DReX-Max, d1-ultra, Microsoft Decision-1, d1 and pplx-decider, which is statistically indistinguishable from every generative judge (0.4–2.3%), but 16.7–49.0% of those of the other nine models, with Mercury-Decide the most vulnerable, compared with 77.3% for a same-size generative judge (Qwen3.5-4B). The checklist lowers this rate for every vulnerable model except Span-02 (Appendix E.5 ). Jev 1.14 also shows the smallest length bias on RM-Bench ( − - 12.9 pp, comparable to GPT-5.6 without reasoning at − - 11.3 pp), whereas the other System-1 models lose 15.0–33.1 points when the rejected answer is the more elaborate one.

sections.heading: Routing with a strong first stage.
sections.text: When Jev or pplx-decider judges every item and low-confidence items are escalated to Opus (thresholds frozen on a development split), routed accuracy on LLMBar reaches 90.7% at 10% escalation and 91.7% at 17% (Opus alone: 91.7%), and on JudgeBench 92.3% at 60% and 91.5% at 41% (Opus: 94.4%), because the confidence of these models identifies their own errors with an AUROC of 0.71–0.90, compared with 0.63–0.81 for Kev-4B (Appendix E.8 ).

sections.heading: Same-size controls.
sections.text: Kev-4B, whose weights and base model are available, allows us to separate the System-1 design from model size. Qwen3.5-4B without thinking is statistically indistinguishable from the Kev-4B checklist on four of five benchmarks, whereas with a 4k-token thinking budget and budget forcing ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) it reaches 84.0% on JudgeBench, 15.7 pp above the Kev-4B checklist ∗ and statistically indistinguishable from the reference-guided Kev-4B, at a median of 117 s per judgment compared with 0.70 s for Kev-4B. The correctness deficit of a small decision model is therefore attributable primarily to the absence of reasoning, and pplx-flash, a 4.5B decision model built on the same base family, shows that a different training recipe recovers part of it without reasoning (72.3% vs. 68.3% on the JudgeBench checklist).

sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: Our results indicate that the choice of decision model matters as much as the choice between System-1 and System-2 judging: under identical questions, the 14 models span 18 points of JudgeBench accuracy and 0–49% attack success. The strongest System-1 judges are viable replacements for a non-reasoning frontier judge on pairwise judgments, particularly when calibrated probabilities are needed, and with a reference generated once per prompt they approach a reasoning judge on correctness and best-of- K K selection at roughly one-sixteenth of the cost, while pointwise checklists are useful mainly for the smaller decision models. Because injection robustness varies by model, it should be measured before a System-1 judge is exposed to text produced by an optimizer or a user, and on long inputs even the strongest System-1 judges trail GPT-5.6 by 10–12 points (Appendix E.12 ). Finally, general System-1 leaderboards provide a useful shortlist for selecting a judge, although neither measures robustness or calibration.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Stronger System-1 models exist: the top entries on the Jev Decision Index and S1MB (e.g., Fastino GLiDE, Jeffan-31B, StartLux-Decision and Darwin-27B) were not evaluated because none is served through the decision-model API we used and self-hosting them requires GPUs with at least 80 GB of memory and model-specific serving code (Appendix B.1 ), so our best-model results are a lower bound on current System-1 judging ability rather than its ceiling. Our catalog inclusion rule also excluded six models on cost or request limits. All results are based on a single run on established benchmarks at pilot scale (80–1,925 items per set), although repeated uncached calls to five hosted decision APIs return the same Choice verdict for 96–100% of 50 JudgeBench requests (Appendix B.4 ), and the relationship between leaderboards and judging accuracy is estimated from 9–12 models, some of which may share training sources with the leaderboards. The injection payloads are our own perturbation of JudgeBench and LLMBar rather than an established injection benchmark, and the checklists and references are produced by Haiku 5.5 and GPT-5.6, so these formulations combine System-1 and System-2 components. Prices are list prices; because the API does not state which GPT-5.6 tier was served, Terra pricing is assumed, and the OpenRouter prices of the System-1 models other than Jev are not reported. Failed calls (rate limits for pplx-flash; context limits for d1-ultra and Microsoft Decision-1 on long inputs) were counted as incorrect. The thinking variant of Qwen3.5-4B was run in a single presentation order and relies on budget forcing for 26–63% of its verdicts, and latencies were measured on a shared laptop GPU.

sections.heading: LLM-as-a-judge.
sections.text: Zheng et al. (2023) introduced MT-Bench and showed that strong LLM judges approach the level of agreement observed between human annotators, while also documenting position bias, verbosity bias and reference-guided grading. Subsequent work has studied probability-weighted scoring ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , open fine-tuned judges ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , generative verifiers ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and judges trained to reason with reinforcement learning ( Whitehouse et al., 2025 ) , and Gu et al. (2024) provide a comprehensive survey of the area. Checklist-based evaluation ( Cook et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) decomposes a judgment into yes/no items written for each instruction; we apply the same idea to a decision model, for which additional questions on the same input add little cost.

sections.heading: Decision models as judges.
sections.text: TypeSafe introduced the System One, or decision-model, category with Jev ( Almeida, 2026 ) , and open models with the same interface followed shortly afterwards, including Kev ( Palmer, 2026 ) , Perplexity’s pplx-decider ( Perplexity AI, 2026 ) and Clef ( Cloudflare, 2026 ) , and a public API catalog now serves dozens of decision models from different providers ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . The S1MB leaderboard ( hotchpotch, 2026 ) and the Jev Decision Index ( multimodalart, 2026 ) rank such models on general decision tasks that contain no judging tasks, which allows us to test whether general decision accuracy predicts judging accuracy. The closest prior work is Li et al. (2026) , who compare Jev with sixteen generative and reward-model judges on pairwise and pointwise correctness tasks, measure calibration and order stability, and study accept-or-escalate cascades; they report, for example, a JudgeBench accuracy of 78.6% for Jev 1.13 (vs. 93.1% for GPT-6) and a frozen cascade that accepts 53.7% of items at a 0.6-point loss. Practitioner write-ups from MLflow (30 items, binary correctness) and Langfuse additionally provide integration guidance ( MLflow, 2026 ; Langfuse, 2026 ) . Our study complements Li et al. (2026) with a comparison across 14 decision models and an analysis of query formulation and checklists, reference-guided grading, injection and bias benchmarks, best-of- K K selection, and scaling, base-model and same-size controls.

sections.heading: Judge biases and attacks.
sections.text: Position bias ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and length bias ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) in LLM judges are well documented. CALM ( Ye et al., 2024 ) quantifies twelve biases through principle-guided perturbations, and EvalBiasBench ( Park et al., 2024 ) provides hand-written pairs for six bias types. Prompt-injection attacks on judges include optimization-based attacks ( Shi et al., 2024 ) and universal adversarial suffixes ( Raina et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We use JudgeBench ( Tan et al., 2024 ) , LLMBar ( Zeng et al., 2023 ) , the MT-Bench human judgments ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) , RM-Bench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , RewardBench 2 ( Malik et al., 2025 ) , the successor to RewardBench ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , HelpSteer2 ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , PPE ( Frick et al., 2024 ) , EvalBiasBench ( Park et al., 2024 ) and CALM ( Ye et al., 2024 ) . We additionally evaluate long-context judging on LongRewardBench ( Tang et al., 2025 ) and agent-trajectory judging on AgentRewardBench ( Lù et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Cascades and calibration.
sections.text: Routing queries between inexpensive and expensive models ( Chen et al., 2023 ) and escalating uncertain judgments with statistical guarantees ( Jung et al., 2024 ) motivate our routing experiments, and we measure calibration with the expected calibration error ( Guo et al., 2017 ) .

sections.heading: Selection of System-1 models.
sections.text: System-1 models had to expose the typed Noul, Choice and Score interface and be either runnable locally as open weights (up to 9B parameters) or served through the OpenRouter decision-model catalog ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . Selection proceeded in two pre-stated stages (Table 2 ). In the first stage, we took the best available model and a size ladder according to the S1MB English leaderboard ( hotchpotch, 2026 ) : Jev 1.14 (S1MB rank 26 of 205), pplx-decider 1.2 (27B, rank 6) and its 4.5B flash variant (rank 35) ( Perplexity AI, 2026 ) , Clef (27B, rank 38) and Clef-flash (9B, rank 68) ( Cloudflare, 2026 ) , and Kev-4B (rank 104) ( Palmer, 2026 ) . In the second stage, we piloted every other entry of the catalog (30 entries on 2026-10-25, listed by the endpoint’s output_modalities=decisions filter) with 100 JudgeBench calls and included every model that handled our requests reliably and whose projected cost for the full suite was at most $4. Jev 1.14 was served as the generally available release ( typesafe/jev-1.14-20261014 ), whereas S1MB lists the preview release, so its S1MB score may differ slightly from that of the model we evaluated. All models other than Kev were called through OpenRouter with the same System One wire format, questions and inputs as Kev, and calls that still failed after three retries (rate-limit errors for a small number of pplx-flash requests) or that the endpoint rejected as too long are counted as incorrect. Two catalog models (mammoth-1, ranked third on the Decision Index, and elephant-1) are served only as free-tier models capped at 1,000 requests per day, which makes a full suite of about 38,000 requests per model infeasible; four exceed the cost cap; one returned server errors for 40% of pilot calls; one rejects our requests; and two return a different output type. sections.heading: Kev-4B as a case study.
sections.text: Kev-4B v1.0 is a LoRA adapter plus pointer head on Qwen3.5-4B-Base ( Palmer, 2026 ; Qwen Team, 2026 ) ; we also run Kev-0.8B and Kev-9B. Its published training mix consists of public classification datasets, generated policy and rule records, consumer-complaint narratives and developer-tooling data, with no human preference data, so every benchmark here is held out for the 0.8B/4B/9B models (the 27B model, which does train on HelpSteer2/3, is not used). All Kev models run locally on an Apple M5 Pro laptop GPU via MLX in bf16 behind the System One API. As a base-model control we serve the untrained Qwen3.5-4B-Base behind the same API, reading next-token probabilities over the same option labels (one prompt format, see Appendix G ).

sections.heading: Generative judges.
sections.text: Through an OpenAI-compatible internal gateway (the development deployment for most runs; the PPE 1–100 rerun and the CALM content audit used the production deployment with the same model identifiers after the development key reached its budget): Claude Haiku 5.5 (thinking disabled), GPT-5.6 with reasoning_effort=none , Claude Opus 5.5 with adaptive thinking at medium effort, and GPT-5.6 at medium reasoning effort. As in ( Li et al., 2026 ) , generative judges get the same rubric and must output only a verdict and a probability, with no rationale. Invalid outputs and gateway errors count as wrong (0.74% of Haiku calls, 0.32% GPT-5.6 without reasoning, 0.14% Opus, 0% GPT-5.6 with reasoning). As a same-size generative control, Qwen3.5-4B was additionally evaluated with thinking disabled and with thinking enabled under a 4,000-token budget with budget forcing ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) , served locally on the same hardware (§ E.11 ).

sections.text: To check that our samples are representative, we ran Jev 1.14, pplx-decider 1.2, DReX-Max and d1-ultra with pairwise Choice in both orders on the full RM-Bench (11,943 pairs) and RB2 (1,763 items, best-of-4) and on JudgeBench’s Claude-generated split (270 pairs), which our main JudgeBench sample (the GPT split) does not include (Table 5 ). sections.heading: B.4 Run-to-run determinism
sections.text: Because every item was judged once, we measured how stable the hosted decision APIs are across repeated calls. For five System-1 models served through OpenRouter, the standard pairwise question set for the first 50 JudgeBench items (canonical order) was sent twice, uncached and under two distinct run names (Table 6 ). The Choice decision was identical in 100% of pairs for four models and in 96% for d1-ultra (47 pairs compared, after three failed calls). The probabilities vary slightly: the mean absolute change in P(A) is 0.007–0.039 (maximum 0.111 for d1-ultra), and pplx-decider 1.2 returned bit-identical probabilities for every request. These results suggest that single-run accuracy estimates are adequate for the decision models, whereas results that depend on probability thresholds, such as routing cutoffs and calibration, carry a small additional noise that is largest for d1-ultra. We did not repeat the generative judges. sections.heading: B.5 Question formulations
sections.text: For a pair, Kev-4B receives the named fields user_request , response_A and response_B and, in a single request, three paraphrased Choice questions, a comparative Noul (“A is better than B”) and two joint Nouls (“A is good” and “B is good”). In the pointwise formulation, each request contains one response and asks a Noul on overall quality, a 6-level Score, six generic checklist Nouls (correctness, final answer, instruction following, completeness, focus and refusal) and three to six item-specific checklist Nouls, which were written once per prompt by Haiku 5.5 under the instruction not to solve the problem. In the reference-guided formulation, GPT-5.6 (medium reasoning) writes one short reference answer per prompt, and Kev-4B is asked in a separate request whether the final answer in the response agrees with that reference. Checklist and pointwise signals are mean logits, pairwise decisions compare the two responses’ signals, and all prompts are listed in Appendix C .

sections.heading: B.6 Statistics, cost and latency
sections.text: 95% CIs are percentile bootstraps over prompts (2,000 resamples) ( Efron and Tibshirani, 1993 ) . Headline comparisons are tested as paired differences on the same items: a prompt-clustered paired bootstrap for CIs and a prompt-level sign-flip permutation test (10,000 each), exact McNemar tests for injection flips, and Holm correction within each pre-defined family of comparisons (six families with 567 tests in total: query formulation 70, injection 180, PPE 120, reference-guided 49, System-1 vs. generative 130 and same-size 18; Appendices D and F ). Long-context and agent-trajectory comparisons are reported with unadjusted bootstrap CIs. “1 call” accuracy averages the two single-order accuracies; “swap” averages probabilities over both orders and then decides. Costs use logged token counts and list prices: Jev and Kev-4B at Jev’s published input-only rate (Kev-4B is free locally), and the OpenRouter prices of the other open models are not reported; Haiku 5.5 $0.10/$0.50, Opus 5.5 $4/$20 and GPT-5.6 $2/$12 per million input/output tokens. The GPT-5.6 tier served by the gateway is not stated, so the Terra list price is an assumption . Latency is measured per request, as server time for Kev-4B on a laptop GPU shared with other jobs and as wall-clock time over the network for the generative judges, and neither measurement constitutes a controlled benchmark. All results are based on a single run.

sections.heading: E.2 How to ask: interfaces and checklists
sections.text: Table 10 and Figure 1 report Kev-4B accuracy for each query formulation. Pairwise A/B Choice is among the weakest formulations, and the comparative Noul (“A is better than B”) is the weakest on every benchmark. Evaluating each response separately and averaging the generic and item-specific checklist Nouls is the best non-reference formulation on LLMBar, RM-Bench and RB2 and is within one point of the best on JudgeBench, improving over swap-averaged Choice by 13.7 pp on RB2 (95% CI [7.7, 20.0]) and 9.3 pp on LLMBar ([5.3, 13.6]), both significant after Holm correction, whereas the differences on RM-Bench (+2.6), JudgeBench (+1.7) and MT-Bench ( − - 1.9) are not significant. The item-specific checklists account for most of the RB2 improvement (70.3% vs. 60.3% for the generic checklist alone), while the generic checklist alone recovers most of the LLMBar improvement (80.9%). Across the 14 decision models (Table 1 ), the checklist helps only the weaker ones: it raises LLMBar accuracy by 8.1–17.2 pp for Clef, pplx-flash, Kev-4B and Clef-flash and RB2 accuracy by 11.0–13.7 pp for DReX v1.5, DReX v2.0, pplx-flash and Kev-4B (all Holm p < 0.05 p<0.05 ), whereas for DReX-Max, d1-ultra, Mercury-Decide and Jev 1.14 it is never significantly different from Choice and for pplx-decider 1.2 it helps only on RM-Bench (+6.9 pp, Holm p < 0.05 p<0.05 ). The checklist therefore appears to compensate for weaknesses of the smaller decision models in pairwise comparison rather than to add information that a strong decision model lacks. sections.heading: Inexpensive ensembles.
sections.text: Averaging over both presentation orders is the only ensemble that improves accuracy on every benchmark (+5.5 pp on JudgeBench, +1.9 on LLMBar, +2.2 on MT-Bench and +1.8 on RM-Bench relative to a single canonical-order call), whereas three paraphrased instructions in both orders (6 calls) add no consistent improvement beyond that ( − - 1.9 to +1.6). In contrast, combining different formulations (swap Choice, Score and checklist, z-scored without fitting) improves accuracy on LLMBar (77.3% vs. 71.8%) and MT-Bench (82.4% vs. 80.2%); the full table is given in Appendix F .

sections.heading: E.3 Reference-guided grading closes the correctness gap
sections.text: On JudgeBench, pairwise Choice reaches only 66.6% with swap averaging, compared with 94.7% for Opus 5.5 with thinking, which is consistent with the multi-hop reasoning weakness that TypeSafe documents for Jev ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ) . Conditioning Kev-4B on a reference answer raises accuracy to 88.0% (Table 11 ), which remains below Opus ( − - 6.7 pp, 95% CI [ − - 10.4, − - 3.3], Holm p p =0.023) but is statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning (+3.6 pp, n.s.) and well above Haiku (+17.9 pp, Holm p < 0.01 p<0.01 ). By source, the reference-guided judge attains 91%, 93%, 79% and 86% on the four JudgeBench sources, close to Opus (92%, 96%, 98% and 94%) except on code. However, the reference helps only when a single correct answer exists: on RB2 Precise IF accuracy drops to 28% (vs. 50% for the checklist) and on Focus to 70% (vs. 93% for Choice), although on RM-Bench the same formulation removes the length bias observed for the other formulations (§ E.6 ). The reference closes the gap for the other decision models as well (Table 1 ): eleven of the 14 models reach 90.3–93.4% on JudgeBench with a reference, which is statistically indistinguishable from Opus ( − - 4.4 to − - 1.3 pp) and GPT-5.6 with reasoning ( − - 2.9 to +0.3 pp), and d1-ultra, pplx-decider, Mercury-Decide, d1, Jev and pplx-flash are significantly more accurate than GPT-5.6 without reasoning (+7.0 to +9.0 pp, Holm p < 0.05 p<0.05 ), whereas Clef-flash (82.0%) and Span-02 (87.1%) remain significantly below both thinking judges. On RB2, reference-guided grading is less accurate than the checklist for eleven of the 14 decision models, since many RB2 items do not have a single checkable answer. sections.heading: Latency.
sections.text: The median Kev-4B server time was 0.70 s per six-question pairwise request and 2.1 s per pointwise request (8 generic and up to 6 item-specific questions) on the laptop GPU, which was shared with other jobs, compared with 0.11 s for Kev-0.8B and 1.8 s for Kev-9B. The generative judges required a median wall-clock time of 1.0 s (Haiku) to 2.7 s (GPT-5.6 with reasoning), although we do not regard these measurements as a controlled latency comparison.

sections.heading: Grader-directed text.
sections.text: We appended one of three payloads to the incorrect response of 150 JudgeBench and 150 LLMBar items: an “evaluator note” claiming that the response had been verified, a fake chat-template system turn, and a plain self-assertion of correctness (Appendix C ). This is a perturbation of established benchmarks rather than an established injection benchmark. Table 13 reports attack success, defined as the share of items judged correctly without the payload that are judged incorrectly with it, and every judge was instructed to ignore claims about grading. The generative judges largely followed this instruction, and their accuracy often increased under injection (Haiku: 74.6% to 88.1% with the evaluator note), which suggests that the payload is treated as evidence against the response. In contrast, the evaluator note reverses 24–33% of Kev-4B’s correct verdicts, and a plain self-assertion shifts its pointwise Score enough to reverse 25.3% of them. Scaling does not mitigate this for pairwise Choice (23% for Kev-0.8B, 32% for 4B and 36% for 9B), although the checklist formulation becomes more robust with size (42%, 24% and 16%). However, the same-size generative judge Qwen3.5-4B is far more vulnerable than Kev-4B (77.3% under the evaluator note; § E.11 ), which indicates that the weakness is shared by small judges in general rather than specific to the System-1 design. The other decision models confirm that susceptibility is model-dependent rather than inherent to the interface (Table 13 ): the evaluator note reverses 0.0–4.7% of the Choice verdicts of DReX-Max, d1-ultra, Microsoft Decision-1, d1 and pplx-decider 1.2, which is statistically indistinguishable from every generative judge (exact McNemar, Holm-adjusted), but 23.3% of Jev 1.14’s and 49.0% of Mercury-Decide’s (both significantly more than every generative judge, Holm p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), while the fake system turn and the self-assertion reverse at most 5.1% of the Choice verdicts of the five most robust models. The checklist formulation lowers the evaluator-note attack success of every model whose Choice attack success exceeds 16% except Span-02, although it raises the fake-system attack success of DReX-Max (5.1% to 21.7%). sections.heading: EvalBiasBench.
sections.text: On the 80 hand-written pairs of EvalBiasBench ( Park et al., 2024 ) , Kev-4B attains 67.5% with Choice and 76.2% with checklists, which is level with Haiku (76.2%) but far below GPT-5.6 and Opus (96–98%). Its errors are concentrated in the empty reference (31–54%) and nested instruction (50–58%) categories, the latter being the benchmark’s counterpart to grader-directed text and therefore consistent with the injection results above. Pointwise grading largely resolves the length-bias items (47% with Choice vs. 94% with checklists). Most of the other decision models perform considerably better with Choice (for example d1-ultra 95.0%, DReX-Max and Microsoft Decision-1 92.5%, Span-02 91.2%, pplx-decider 1.2 90.0% and Jev 1.14 88.8%), approaching GPT-5.6 and Opus, whereas Clef reaches only 60.0% with Choice and 83.8% with checklists.

sections.heading: CALM.
sections.text: We use the four released CALM bias sets with the perturbed answers provided by the authors ( Ye et al., 2024 ) , while the assignment of each perturbation to the chosen or rejected answer is our own (Appendix H ). Table 14 reports the robustness rate (RR), defined as the share of verdicts that remain unchanged under a content-preserving perturbation. Fake citations change approximately 30% of verdicts for every generative judge, including Opus with thinking (RR 69–73), whereas Kev-4B Choice is the most robust judge (RR 75–83). Rewriting the better answer in an angry, fearful or sad tone reverses most generative verdicts (RR 9–42), and while Kev-4B pointwise scoring is considerably more robust to these rewrites (RR 44–70), Kev-4B Choice is not (RR 7–40). In CALM’s fallacy set, flawed reasoning is inserted into the better answer, so a reliable judge should change its verdict, and Kev-4B Choice detects the inserted fallacy 97% of the time, matching Haiku (97%) and exceeding Opus (93%). A longer rejected answer has little effect on pairwise verdicts (RR 94–99) and a slightly larger effect on Kev-4B pointwise scoring (RR 85–89). To verify that the released rewrites preserve content, GPT-5.6 and Opus 5.5 (both with thinking) independently compared every rewrite with its original, and a rewrite was retained only if both auditors judged its final answer and substance unchanged (or, for the fallacy set, judged its substance worse). Between 83% and 100% of the rewrites pass for every variant except the quote-based authority rewrite, of which only 6% pass (auditor agreement 55%), so that column should be regarded as unreliable. On the audited items, the robustness rates change by at most a few points (for example, 9% to 9% for GPT-5.6 without reasoning on angry rewrites and 42% to 43% for Opus on sad rewrites), which confirms that the sentiment effect reflects a judge bias rather than an artifact of the rewrites. The other decision models (Jev 1.14, pplx-decider 1.2, pplx-flash and Clef-flash) show the same pattern with Choice: they are at least as robust as every generative judge to fake citations (RR 72–82 vs. 65–73), detect the inserted fallacies 95–98% of the time, and are strongly affected by sentiment rewrites of the better answer (RR 11–60), so the sentiment vulnerability is shared by both judge types. sections.heading: E.6 Length and position
sections.text: On RM-Bench (Table 15 ), Kev-4B Choice loses 26.0 points when the rejected answer is the more elaborate one, compared with 8.7–19.2 points for the generative judges. Pointwise scoring reduces this gap by roughly half ( − - 12.2), and reference-guided grading removes it (+1.9), which indicates that stylistic differences no longer influence the judgment once the question is whether the final answer matches a reference. The same holds for Jev 1.14 ( − - 0.1 with a reference vs. − - 12.9 with Choice), and the checklist reduces pplx-decider’s gap from − - 23.3 to − - 9.6. Position sensitivity is larger for Kev-4B than for any generative judge: Kev-4B changes its verdict under order swap on 15.5–19.8% of LLMBar, MT-Bench and RM-Bench pairs and on 38.6% of JudgeBench pairs, compared with 7.7–28.9% for the other decision models (Table 8 ), 29.3% for Haiku, 9.7% for GPT-5.6 without reasoning and 1.4–2.6% for the thinking judges on JudgeBench, whereas pointwise formulations are unaffected by presentation order by construction. sections.heading: E.7 Absolute grading and calibration
sections.text: Against human HelpSteer2 helpfulness ratings, every generative judge reaches Spearman ρ \rho 0.43–0.44 with overlapping CIs, from Haiku to Opus with thinking. Kev-4B Score reaches 0.315 [0.20,0.42] , and checklists do not help (0.288). We interpreted this common ceiling as a consequence of noise in the human labels; however, six System-1 models exceed it with their pointwise Score (pplx-decider 1.2 0.498 [0.39,0.59] , DReX-Max 0.492, Microsoft Decision-1 0.490, d1-ultra 0.488, d1 0.454 and Mercury-Decide 0.445), which suggests that the ceiling is not entirely due to label noise, although the confidence intervals overlap. Jev 1.14 (0.410) and pplx-flash (0.420) are level with the generative judges, while Kev-4B and Clef-flash (0.252–0.315) are below them, consistent with TypeSafe’s note that Score levels are weakly calibrated ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ) . For the calibration of the A/B probability (single call, pooled across pairwise benchmarks), Jev 1.14 attains the lowest ECE of any judge (0.019, Brier 0.119), followed by DReX-Max (0.024), d1-ultra (0.030), d1 (0.031) and pplx-decider 1.2 (0.038), whereas Clef is the least calibrated (0.132). Kev-4B attains an ECE of 0.058, which is similar to the verbalized confidence of Haiku (0.056) and better than that of GPT-5.6 without reasoning (0.075) and Opus (0.087), although its Brier score (0.184) is higher because it is less accurate.

sections.heading: E.8 Routing uncertain cases to a stronger judge
sections.text: In the routing setting, a System-1 model (Kev-4B, Jev 1.14 or pplx-decider 1.2) judges every item first, and items whose confidence falls below a threshold τ \tau are escalated to a generative judge. Prompts were split 30/70 into development and test sets, and τ \tau was set to the lowest threshold whose development accuracy is within one point of the fallback’s, then frozen before evaluation on the test set. The Kev-4B confidence signal is the z-scored sum of the swap Choice, Score and checklist margins, with forced escalation whenever the two presentation orders disagree. As shown in Table 16 and Figure 3 , routing outperforms random escalation at the same rate by 1.5–5 points but remains far from the oracle: on LLMBar it comes within one point of Opus while still escalating 80% of items, and on JudgeBench it falls five points short at 67% escalation. On RB2, the development threshold did not transfer (16% escalated, 17 points short), because the 78-item development split happened to be easier than the test split, and thresholds fitted on the other benchmarks escalated anywhere from 33% to 100% of items. The error-detection AUROC of Kev-4B confidence is 0.63–0.66 on JudgeBench, 0.67–0.71 on LLMBar, 0.70–0.74 on MT-Bench and RM-Bench, and 0.81 on RB2, and a logistic-regression router over seven Kev-4B signals fitted on the pooled development data does not improve test AUROC (0.61–0.73 vs. 0.63–0.72). MT-Bench is the exception, since Kev-4B alone matches GPT-5.6 without reasoning (83.0% vs. 83.5%) and the best policy is therefore never to escalate, at approximately 10% of the cost.

sections.heading: Strong first stages.
sections.text: With Jev 1.14 or pplx-decider 1.2 as the first stage, the same frozen-threshold procedure is considerably more useful (Table 16 ): on LLMBar, the routed judge reaches 90.7% with Jev at 10% escalation and 91.7% with pplx-decider at 17% escalation (Opus alone: 91.7%), at 15% and 21% of Opus’s cost, and on JudgeBench it reaches 92.3% (Jev, 60% escalated) and 91.5% (pplx-decider, 41%) compared with 94.4% for Opus. Both models identify their own errors far better than Kev-4B, with an error-detection AUROC of 0.71–0.88 for Jev and 0.71–0.90 for pplx-decider across the five pairwise benchmarks (vs. 0.63–0.81 for Kev-4B). On RB2, however, the development threshold again did not transfer for Jev (no items escalated), so a few hundred labeled items from the target distribution remain necessary to set τ \tau . These results indicate that routing pays off when the first-stage System-1 model is both strong and well calibrated, whereas for a weak first stage most items must be escalated. sections.heading: E.9 Scaling and the base-model control
sections.text: Table 17 and Figure 4 summarize the scaling and base-model results. Kev-0.8B performs near chance and is not usable as a judge, while scaling from 4B to 9B adds 0–3 points on every formulation, so that Kev-9B matches Haiku on JudgeBench (69% vs. 70%), surpasses it with checklists on LLMBar (81% vs. 74%) and trails it on RB2 (73% vs. 76%); notably, the JudgeBench flip rate does not decrease with size (38–39%). Relative to the untrained base model served behind the same API, decision training yields large gains on LLMBar (+21.9 pp with Choice and +15.7 pp with checklists) and in checklist accuracy (+12.3 pp on RB2 and +10.6 pp on JudgeBench), and it substantially improves calibration (ECE from 0.204 to 0.058). sections.heading: E.10 Best-of- K K selection on PPE
sections.text: PPE’s best-of- K K sets ( Frick et al., 2024 ) pair each prompt with many sampled responses and verifiable correctness labels. We use 60 prompts per domain whose first 16 responses are mixed (47.5% correct on average) and report the probability that the top-ranked response is correct, splitting ties at the top evenly (Table 18 ); the generative judges score each response on a 1–100 scale. On the three single-answer domains, the reference-guided Kev-4B reaches 87.2%, which is statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 with reasoning (91.2%; − - 4.0 pp, 95% CI [ − - 8.5, +0.1]) and from Opus with thinking (94.6%; − - 7.4 pp, Holm p p =0.052) and significantly higher than Haiku (+11.5 pp) and GPT-5.6 without reasoning (+12.8 pp). Because one GPT-5.6 reference and sixteen Kev-4B calls cost $0.0049 per prompt, compared with $0.0827 for GPT-5.6 with reasoning, $0.1308 for Opus and $0.0027 for Haiku, the reference-guided judge recovers approximately 96% of GPT-5.6’s best-of-16 accuracy at about one-seventeenth of the cost. In contrast, the reference-free Kev-4B checklist (67.3% overall) is significantly less accurate than GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning and Opus ( − - 10.8 to − - 23.4 pp). An earlier run in which the generative judges used a 1–6 scale produced heavy ties (on average 10.2–14.6 of the 16 responses shared the top score) and placed Opus at 67.3%, level with the Kev-4B checklist; on the 1–100 scale the number of tied responses falls to 1.9–3.7 and pairwise discrimination between correct and incorrect responses rises from 51–68% to 72–91%, which indicates that coarse integer scales are unsuitable for best-of- K K evaluation. Neither Kev-4B nor the generative judges show a meaningful length preference in their selections (within-prompt Spearman ρ \rho between − - 0.02 and +0.06), and 221 of Haiku’s 4,800 outputs could not be parsed and were treated as never top-ranked.

sections.text: The reference-guided recipe transfers to every decision model we evaluated. With one GPT-5.6 reference and sixteen Jev calls, the reference-guided Jev costs $0.0051 per prompt, or approximately one-sixteenth of the cost of GPT-5.6 with reasoning. Without a reference, the best System-1 checklist (DReX-Max, 79.3%) is statistically indistinguishable from Haiku and GPT-5.6 without reasoning but significantly below GPT-5.6 with reasoning ( − - 8.4 pp, 95% CI [ − - 13.5, − - 3.4]) and Opus ( − - 11.4 pp), and every System-1 checklist is significantly below Opus, which confirms that the reference, rather than the choice of decision model, determines whether a System-1 judge is competitive for best-of- K K selection on verifiable tasks. sections.heading: E.11 Same-size generative control
sections.text: To separate the effect of the System-1 design from the effect of model size, we evaluated Qwen3.5-4B, the instruction-tuned counterpart of Kev-4B’s base model, as a generative judge with thinking disabled, using the same rubric, the same verdict-only output format and the same hardware (served locally through mlx_lm ). All 5,638 pairwise and best-of-4 calls returned a valid verdict. Table 19 compares it with Kev-4B. Averaged over both presentation orders, Qwen3.5-4B is statistically indistinguishable from the Kev-4B checklist formulation on JudgeBench, MT-Bench, RM-Bench and RB2 (paired differences of − - 3.2 to +3.0 pp, all n.s.), whereas the Kev-4B checklist is 13.8 pp more accurate on LLMBar (95% CI [9.3, 18.4], Holm p < 0.01 p<0.01 ) and Kev-4B’s pairwise Choice is 15.0 pp less accurate than Qwen3.5-4B on RB2 ([ − - 20.3, − - 9.7], Holm p < 0.01 p<0.01 ). Qwen3.5-4B is also more sensitive to presentation order (43.1% of JudgeBench verdicts change under swap, vs. 38.6% for Kev-4B) and considerably more vulnerable to injected instructions, since the evaluator note reverses 77.3% of its correct verdicts and the fake system turn 42.8%, compared with 32.2% and 8.8% for Kev-4B Choice. These results suggest that, at equal size, the decision model’s advantage lies less in raw accuracy than in calibrated probabilities, inexpensive multi-question checklists and lower susceptibility to grader-directed text, and that the injection weakness reported in § E.5 is primarily a property of small judges. The thinking variant of Qwen3.5-4B was evaluated with a total budget of 4,000 tokens in a single presentation order; when no verdict had been produced within the budget, budget forcing ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) closed the reasoning block over the partial reasoning and required an answer. All 1,069 calls produced a valid verdict, and the model reaches 84.0% on JudgeBench (95% CI [80, 88]), 84.7% on LLMBar ([81, 88]) and 85.0% on RB2 ([81, 89]), with 63%, 26% and 42% of verdicts forced, respectively. Forced verdicts are less accurate than natural ones on LLMBar (70.9% vs. 89.6%) and RB2 (78.4% vs. 89.7%) but only slightly so on JudgeBench (82.8% vs. 86.0%). Relative to Kev-4B, the thinking judge is 15.7 pp more accurate than the checklist formulation on JudgeBench and 14.0 pp more accurate on RB2 (both Holm p < 0.01 p<0.01 ), whereas the differences from the checklist on LLMBar ( − - 3.6 pp) and from the reference-guided Kev-4B on JudgeBench (+4.0 pp in favor of Kev-4B) are not significant. Together with the non-thinking results, this indicates that the decision model’s deficit on hard correctness judgments is attributable primarily to the absence of reasoning rather than to model size, since the same 4B model with thinking matches GPT-5.6 without reasoning on JudgeBench (84.0% vs. 84.4%). However, this accuracy comes at a substantial latency cost: the thinking judge required a median of 117 s per judgment on the shared laptop GPU (median 3,319 thinking tokens), compared with 0.70 s for Kev-4B, or approximately 170 × \times longer. sections.heading: E.12 Long-context judging
sections.text: LongRewardBench ( Tang et al., 2025 ) pairs long contexts with two candidate responses across seven tasks. We sampled up to 60 pairwise items per length bucket from 4K to 64K tokens, stratified over tasks ( n = 243 n=243 after deduplication: 59, 59, 57, 51 and 17 items), and evaluated Kev-4B Choice and Haiku in both orders and GPT-5.6 and Opus in the canonical order only. Because Kev-4B refuses states longer than 65,536 tokens, 27 items (mostly in the 64K bucket) could not be scored and are counted as incorrect in the main comparison, and we additionally report results on the 216 items that Kev-4B could score (Table 20 ). At 4K, Kev-4B (78.0%) is statistically indistinguishable from every generative judge ( − - 6.8 to +4.2 pp, all n.s.), but its accuracy falls by approximately 20 points at 8K and continues to decline to 44.4% at 64K (on 9 items), whereas GPT-5.6 remains at approximately 81% across buckets. On the 216 scorable items, Kev-4B (62.5%) is significantly less accurate than Haiku ( − - 8.6 pp, 95% CI [ − - 16.2, − - 0.9]), Opus ( − - 9.7 pp) and GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning ( − - 19.4 and − - 18.5 pp). The stronger decision models degrade less with length (Table 20 ): over all 243 items, Jev 1.14 and pplx-decider 1.2 both reach 70.8%, which is statistically indistinguishable from Haiku ( − - 2.3 pp) and Opus ( − - 1.0 pp) but significantly below GPT-5.6 without and with reasoning ( − - 10.5 pp, 95% CI [ − - 15.2, − - 5.8], and − - 11.9 pp, [ − - 16.9, − - 7.0]), and 15.2 pp above Kev-4B. pplx-flash reaches 63.8% (70.1% on the 221 items it answered, since 22 calls failed with rate-limit errors), whereas the endpoint rejected 72 of Clef-flash’s 243 items as too long and its accuracy on the remaining items (43.9%) is close to chance. These results are consistent with the distractor and large-state weaknesses that TypeSafe documents for Jev ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ) , and they suggest that relevant spans should be retrieved or filtered before a smaller decision model is queried on long inputs, although the 64K bucket is too small for firm conclusions. Among the other decision models, DReX-Max (69.8%) and Span-02 (68.7%) are statistically indistinguishable from Haiku and Opus but significantly below GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning ( − - 11.5 to − - 14.0 pp), and Mercury-Decide is the most accurate System-1 model on the 216 items within Kev-4B’s limit (72.7%) but failed on 27 longer items. d1-ultra and Microsoft Decision-1 have 32K-token context windows, so most of their 32K and 64K items are rejected as too long (both 0% at 64K), and their overall accuracy (45.5–45.9%) reflects context limits rather than judging ability; on the items they answered, they reach 73.8% and 70.4%. sections.heading: E.13 Judging agent trajectories
sections.text: AgentRewardBench ( Lù et al., 2025 ) provides expert labels for whether a web agent succeeded, caused unintended side effects or repeated actions unnecessarily. We used the test split with the first annotation per trajectory and excluded “unsure” labels, which yields 292 trajectories from WebArena (100), WorkArena (100) and VisualWebArena (92), of which 32% are successful. Every judge receives the goal, the sequence of steps (URL, action and the agent’s reasoning truncated to 400 characters) and the final page’s pruned accessibility tree truncated to 12,000 characters, without screenshots; Kev-4B answers three Nouls in a single request, and the generative judges return a success probability together with binary side-effect and looping judgments. At a threshold of 0.5, Kev-4B attains the highest success F1 (75.0%, 95% CI [67.9, 81.1]) and recall (88.0%) but the lowest precision (65.3%), whereas the generative judges are conservative, with precision of 77–89% and recall of 35–65% (Table 21 ). However, this F1 advantage reflects the operating point rather than better discrimination: the threshold-free AUROC of Kev-4B (0.887) is statistically indistinguishable from that of Haiku (+0.013) and GPT-5.6 without reasoning ( − - 0.021) but significantly below GPT-5.6 with reasoning ( − - 0.032, 95% CI [ − - 0.064, − - 0.000]) and Opus ( − - 0.046, [ − - 0.084, − - 0.012]), and when its threshold is raised to match the precision of GPT-5.6 with reasoning (81.8%), its recall falls to 29.3%. Since Lù et al. (2025) emphasize precision for this task, the threshold of a decision-model judge should be chosen for the intended operating point. Side effects are difficult for every judge (F1 of 27–34% for the generative judges), and Kev-4B’s side-effect probability never exceeds 0.425, so it predicts no side effects at a threshold of 0.5 (AUROC 0.617 against 19 positives), whereas looping is detected reliably by all judges (F1 84–90%; Kev-4B AUROC 0.930). Among the other decision models, pplx-decider 1.2 attains the highest System-1 AUROC (0.921), which is statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 with reasoning (+0.003, 95% CI [ − - 0.017, +0.023]) and Opus ( − - 0.012, [ − - 0.032, +0.007]) and significantly above Haiku (+0.047), at a balanced operating point (precision 77.4%, recall 70.7%, F1 73.9%). Jev 1.14 (0.895) is conservative at a threshold of 0.5 (precision 87.5%, recall 53.3%) and is significantly below Opus only ( − - 0.038, [ − - 0.067, − - 0.012]), whereas pplx-flash and Clef-flash (both 0.870) are significantly below GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning and Opus. Of the models added in the catalog sweep, d1-ultra (0.915) and DReX-Max (0.908) are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and d1-ultra is also indistinguishable from Opus ( − - 0.018, [ − - 0.041, +0.001]), whereas Microsoft Decision-1, Span-02 and both earlier DReX versions are significantly below GPT-5.6 with reasoning and Opus. sections.heading: Appendix G Base-model reader
sections.text: The base-model control serves Qwen3.5-4B-Base behind the System One API. The state is rendered as ### <field> blocks and prefilled once; for each question the cached state is copied and a suffix is appended with the question, the options as label: description lines, and Answer: . Probabilities are the softmax over the first token of each “ label” (yes/no for Nouls, 1..N for Scores, option keys for Choices). We verified that the copied-cache answer equals a full recomputation on a test prompt.

sections.heading: Appendix H CALM variant selection
sections.text: From each CALM set we sample 150 base items (seed 12) and use the authors’ perturbed answers: authority, the rejected answer with a book, quote or URL reference added; verbosity, the rejected answer lengthened; sentiment, the chosen answer rewritten angry, fearful or sad, and the rejected answer rewritten cheerful; fallacy oversight, the chosen answer with inserted fallacious reasoning. Each base item keeps one fixed A/B assignment across its variants.

Shreyas Subramanian Affiliation: Scale AI Abstract Decision models such as TypeSafe’s Jev answer typed questions about a text (yes/no, multiple choice, or an ordinal score) with calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass and without generating text, which makes them an inexpensive candidate for LLM-as-a-judge workloads. We evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol from an independent leaderboard and from every entry of a public decision-model catalog, against four generative judges (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking) on eleven established judge benchmarks. Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and the two strongest, DReX-Max and d1-ultra, are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2 (+10.5 to +14.4 pp). Conditioned on a reference answer generated once per prompt, eleven models reach 90.3–93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning, and on PPE best-of-16 every reference-guided System-1 judge is statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 with reasoning (87.2–92.8% vs. 91.2%), at approximately one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt for Jev. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge (ECE 0.019–0.031 vs. 0.038–0.087) and correlate more strongly with human helpfulness ratings ( ρ \rho up to 0.50 vs. 0.43–0.44). Robustness to instructions injected into the judged response is a property of the individual model rather than of the System-1 design, since an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0.0–4.7% of the correct verdicts of five models, statistically indistinguishable from the generative judges, but 16.7–49.0% of those of the other nine. Finally, two general System-1 leaderboards that contain no judging tasks predict judging accuracy (Pearson r r = 0.95–0.96), a well-calibrated System-1 first stage matches Opus on LLMBar while escalating 17% of items, and same-size controls show that the correctness deficit of a 4B decision model is a reasoning gap rather than a size gap. 1 Introduction LLM judges are now widely used for model evaluation, data filtering and reward modeling ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) ; however, frontier judges with extended reasoning are slow and expensive when they are called thousands of times per batch, as in best-of- N N sampling or reinforcement learning. TypeSafe recently introduced Jev as a System One decision model ( Almeida, 2026 ) , which takes a state together with typed questions (a yes/no Noul , a Choice over named options, or an ordinal Score ) and returns a probability for every question in parallel, and many decision models with the same interface have since been released, several of them through a common API catalog ( Palmer, 2026 ; Perplexity AI, 2026 ; Cloudflare, 2026 ; OpenRouter, 2026 ) . Li et al. (2026) evaluated an earlier Jev release as a pairwise judge and found it competitive on ordinary preference judgments but 9–20 points behind frontier judges when correctness has to be verified. Despite this initial evidence, it remains unclear how much the accuracy of a System-1 judge depends on the particular decision model, how such a model should be queried, and which of its failure modes are specific to the System-1 design rather than to model size. In this study we evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, including Jev 1.14, with identical questions and inputs on established benchmarks only, and compare them with four generative judges. Our main contributions are as follows: (1) we show that the strongest System-1 judges match GPT-5.6 without reasoning on pairwise judgments and that general System-1 leaderboards predict judging accuracy across models; (2) we show that a per-prompt reference answer brings System-1 judges to the level of reasoning judges on correctness and best-of- K K selection at a small fraction of the cost; (3) we show that pointwise checklists help only the weaker models and that robustness to injected instructions is a per-model property; (4) we show that a strong, well-calibrated System-1 first stage makes escalation to a frontier judge worthwhile; and (5) using a 4B decision model with same-size generative controls, we show that its remaining correctness deficit reflects the absence of reasoning rather than model size. Related work is discussed in Appendix A , and further results are reported in Appendix E . 2 Methodology Models. System-1 models had to expose the typed Noul, Choice and Score interface and be either runnable locally as open weights (up to 9B parameters) or served through the OpenRouter decision-model catalog ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . We first took the best available model and a size ladder according to the S1MB English leaderboard ( hotchpotch, 2026 ) : Jev 1.14, pplx-decider 1.2 and pplx-flash 1.2 ( Perplexity AI, 2026 ) , Clef and Clef-flash ( Cloudflare, 2026 ) , and Kev-4B ( Palmer, 2026 ) , which runs locally through MLX. We then piloted every other catalog entry (30 on 2026-10-25) with 100 JudgeBench calls and included those that handled our requests reliably at a projected full-suite cost of at most $4: d1 and d1-ultra, Mercury-Decide, Microsoft Decision-1, DReX v1.5, v2.0 and Max, and Span-02. All 14 models were run on the full benchmark suite; Kev-0.8B, Kev-9B and the untrained Qwen3.5-4B-Base form a scaling ablation on a subset, and excluded or higher-ranked models are listed in Appendix B.1 . The generative judges received the same rubric (Appendix C ) and, following Li et al. (2026) , output only a verdict and a probability. Benchmarks. We use JudgeBench ( Tan et al., 2024 , 350 pairs) , LLMBar ( Zeng et al., 2023 , 419) , the MT-Bench human judgments ( Zheng et al., 2023 , 313 non-tie pairs) , RM-Bench ( Liu et al., 2024 , 1,350) , RewardBench 2 in its best-of-4 format ( Malik et al., 2025 , RB2, 300) , PPE best-of- K K ( Frick et al., 2024 , 300 prompts with 16 responses each) and HelpSteer2 ( Wang et al., 2024 , 300 responses with human ratings) , with EvalBiasBench, CALM, LongRewardBench and AgentRewardBench reported in Appendix E . Every pairwise item was evaluated in both presentation orders, and for Jev, pplx-decider, DReX-Max and d1-ultra the full RM-Bench (11,943 pairs) and RB2 (1,763) sets agree with our samples within 2.3 pp, with DReX-Max and d1-ultra ahead of Jev and pplx-decider on every full set (Appendix B.3 ). Query formulations. In the pairwise Choice formulation, a decision model receives the fields user_request , response_A and response_B with an A/B Choice question, and probabilities are averaged over both orders. In the checklist formulation, each response is evaluated in a separate request with six generic Nouls (correctness, final answer, instruction following, completeness, focus and refusal) and three to six item-specific Nouls written once per prompt by Haiku 5.5, and the signal is the mean logit. In the reference-guided formulation, GPT-5.6 writes one short reference answer per prompt and the decision model is asked whether a response’s final answer agrees with it. Statistical testing. Paired differences are reported with 95% confidence intervals from a prompt-clustered bootstrap and p p -values from a prompt-level sign-flip permutation test (exact McNemar for injection), with Holm correction within each pre-defined family of comparisons (Appendix D ); ∗ denotes a Holm-adjusted p < 0.05 p<0.05 . 3 Results JudgeBench LLMBar RB2 (best-of-4) MT RM PPE Note Judge Choice Checkl. + ref Choice Checkl. Accuracy across System-1 models. Accuracy varies widely across the 14 decision models (Table 1 ): with pairwise Choice, JudgeBench accuracy ranges from 66.6% (Kev-4B) to 84.6% (d1-ultra) and RB2 accuracy from 57.3% to 87.0% (DReX-Max). Five models (DReX-Max, d1-ultra, Mercury-Decide, Jev 1.14 and pplx-decider 1.2) are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks (differences of − - 6.6 to +4.3 pp, all n.s.), and DReX-Max and d1-ultra are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RB2 (+10.5 to +14.4 pp ∗ ). The strongest models are also far less sensitive to presentation order than Kev-4B (7.7–12.9% vs. 38.6% of JudgeBench verdicts change under swap). General System-1 leaderboards, which contain no judging tasks, predict judging accuracy: the mean Choice accuracy over JudgeBench, LLMBar and RB2 correlates with the Jev Decision Index ( multimodalart, 2026 ) at Pearson r r = 0.96 over 12 models (0.89 without the Kev models, whose leaderboard entries are later revisions) and with S1MB at r r = 0.95 over nine (0.78), and the two leaderboards agree with each other ( r r = 0.97), which suggests that either provides a useful shortlist for selecting a System-1 judge (Appendix E.1 ). Effect of query formulation. Pointwise checklists improve only the weaker models: they raise LLMBar accuracy by 8.1–17.2 pp for Clef, pplx-flash, Kev-4B and Clef-flash and RB2 accuracy by 11.0–13.7 pp for DReX v1.5, DReX v2.0, pplx-flash and Kev-4B (all ∗ ), whereas for the five strongest models the checklist is never significantly better than Choice except for pplx-decider on RM-Bench (+6.9 pp ∗ ). Because additional questions on the same state add little cost, the checklist formulation costs one Haiku call per prompt ($0.16 per 1,000 prompts) in addition to the decision model’s input tokens, which makes it most attractive for the smaller and less accurate decision models. Reference-guided grading and best-of- K K selection. Conditioning on a reference answer closes most of the remaining correctness gap: on JudgeBench, eleven of the 14 models reach 90.3–93.4%, which is statistically indistinguishable from Opus (94.7%) and GPT-5.6 with reasoning (93.1%), and six of them (d1-ultra, pplx-decider, Mercury-Decide, d1, Jev and pplx-flash) are significantly more accurate than GPT-5.6 without reasoning (+7.0 to +9.0 pp ∗ ). On PPE best-of-16, where one reference is shared by sixteen responses, every reference-guided System-1 judge is statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 with reasoning (87.2–92.8% vs. 91.2%), all except Clef-flash are also indistinguishable from Opus (94.6%), and all 14 are significantly more accurate than Haiku and GPT-5.6 without reasoning (75.7% and 74.4%). With one GPT-5.6 reference and sixteen Jev calls this costs $0.0051 per prompt, compared with $0.0827 for GPT-5.6 with reasoning and $0.1308 for Opus. Without a reference, the best System-1 checklist (DReX-Max, 79.3%) matches Haiku and GPT-5.6 without reasoning but remains significantly below GPT-5.6 with reasoning and Opus ( − - 8.4 and − - 11.4 pp ∗ ; Appendix E.10 ). Calibration, human agreement and robustness. Jev 1.14 attains the lowest calibration error of any judge (ECE 0.019), and DReX-Max, d1-ultra and d1 (0.024–0.031) are also better calibrated than every generative judge (0.038–0.087). Six System-1 models correlate more strongly with human HelpSteer2 helpfulness ratings than every generative judge (Spearman ρ \rho = 0.445–0.498 vs. 0.43–0.44), although the confidence intervals overlap. Robustness to grader-directed text is a property of the individual model: an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0.0–4.7% of the correct Choice verdicts of DReX-Max, d1-ultra, Microsoft Decision-1, d1 and pplx-decider, which is statistically indistinguishable from every generative judge (0.4–2.3%), but 16.7–49.0% of those of the other nine models, with Mercury-Decide the most vulnerable, compared with 77.3% for a same-size generative judge (Qwen3.5-4B). The checklist lowers this rate for every vulnerable model except Span-02 (Appendix E.5 ). Jev 1.14 also shows the smallest length bias on RM-Bench ( − - 12.9 pp, comparable to GPT-5.6 without reasoning at − - 11.3 pp), whereas the other System-1 models lose 15.0–33.1 points when the rejected answer is the more elaborate one. Routing with a strong first stage. When Jev or pplx-decider judges every item and low-confidence items are escalated to Opus (thresholds frozen on a development split), routed accuracy on LLMBar reaches 90.7% at 10% escalation and 91.7% at 17% (Opus alone: 91.7%), and on JudgeBench 92.3% at 60% and 91.5% at 41% (Opus: 94.4%), because the confidence of these models identifies their own errors with an AUROC of 0.71–0.90, compared with 0.63–0.81 for Kev-4B (Appendix E.8 ). Same-size controls. Kev-4B, whose weights and base model are available, allows us to separate the System-1 design from model size. Qwen3.5-4B without thinking is statistically indistinguishable from the Kev-4B checklist on four of five benchmarks, whereas with a 4k-token thinking budget and budget forcing ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) it reaches 84.0% on JudgeBench, 15.7 pp above the Kev-4B checklist ∗ and statistically indistinguishable from the reference-guided Kev-4B, at a median of 117 s per judgment compared with 0.70 s for Kev-4B. The correctness deficit of a small decision model is therefore attributable primarily to the absence of reasoning, and pplx-flash, a 4.5B decision model built on the same base family, shows that a different training recipe recovers part of it without reasoning (72.3% vs. 68.3% on the JudgeBench checklist). 4 Discussion Our results indicate that the choice of decision model matters as much as the choice between System-1 and System-2 judging: under identical questions, the 14 models span 18 points of JudgeBench accuracy and 0–49% attack success. The strongest System-1 judges are viable replacements for a non-reasoning frontier judge on pairwise judgments, particularly when calibrated probabilities are needed, and with a reference generated once per prompt they approach a reasoning judge on correctness and best-of- K K selection at roughly one-sixteenth of the cost, while pointwise checklists are useful mainly for the smaller decision models. Because injection robustness varies by model, it should be measured before a System-1 judge is exposed to text produced by an optimizer or a user, and on long inputs even the strongest System-1 judges trail GPT-5.6 by 10–12 points (Appendix E.12 ). Finally, general System-1 leaderboards provide a useful shortlist for selecting a judge, although neither measures robustness or calibration. Limitations Stronger System-1 models exist: the top entries on the Jev Decision Index and S1MB (e.g., Fastino GLiDE, Jeffan-31B, StartLux-Decision and Darwin-27B) were not evaluated because none is served through the decision-model API we used and self-hosting them requires GPUs with at least 80 GB of memory and model-specific serving code (Appendix B.1 ), so our best-model results are a lower bound on current System-1 judging ability rather than its ceiling. Our catalog inclusion rule also excluded six models on cost or request limits. All results are based on a single run on established benchmarks at pilot scale (80–1,925 items per set), although repeated uncached calls to five hosted decision APIs return the same Choice verdict for 96–100% of 50 JudgeBench requests (Appendix B.4 ), and the relationship between leaderboards and judging accuracy is estimated from 9–12 models, some of which may share training sources with the leaderboards. The injection payloads are our own perturbation of JudgeBench and LLMBar rather than an established injection benchmark, and the checklists and references are produced by Haiku 5.5 and GPT-5.6, so these formulations combine System-1 and System-2 components. Prices are list prices; because the API does not state which GPT-5.6 tier was served, Terra pricing is assumed, and the OpenRouter prices of the System-1 models other than Jev are not reported. Failed calls (rate limits for pplx-flash; context limits for d1-ultra and Microsoft Decision-1 on long inputs) were counted as incorrect. The thinking variant of Qwen3.5-4B was run in a single presentation order and relies on budget forcing for 26–63% of its verdicts, and latencies were measured on a shared laptop GPU. (2023) introduced MT-Bench and showed that strong LLM judges approach the level of agreement observed between human annotators, while also documenting position bias, verbosity bias and reference-guided grading. Subsequent work has studied probability-weighted scoring ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , open fine-tuned judges ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , generative verifiers ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and judges trained to reason with reinforcement learning ( Whitehouse et al., 2025 ) , and Gu et al. (2024) provide a comprehensive survey of the area. Checklist-based evaluation ( Cook et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) decomposes a judgment into yes/no items written for each instruction; we apply the same idea to a decision model, for which additional questions on the same input add little cost. Decision models as judges. TypeSafe introduced the System One, or decision-model, category with Jev ( Almeida, 2026 ) , and open models with the same interface followed shortly afterwards, including Kev ( Palmer, 2026 ) , Perplexity’s pplx-decider ( Perplexity AI, 2026 ) and Clef ( Cloudflare, 2026 ) , and a public API catalog now serves dozens of decision models from different providers ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . The S1MB leaderboard ( hotchpotch, 2026 ) and the Jev Decision Index ( multimodalart, 2026 ) rank such models on general decision tasks that contain no judging tasks, which allows us to test whether general decision accuracy predicts judging accuracy. The closest prior work is Li et al. (2026) , who compare Jev with sixteen generative and reward-model judges on pairwise and pointwise correctness tasks, measure calibration and order stability, and study accept-or-escalate cascades; they report, for example, a JudgeBench accuracy of 78.6% for Jev 1.13 (vs. 93.1% for GPT-6) and a frozen cascade that accepts 53.7% of items at a 0.6-point loss. Practitioner write-ups from MLflow (30 items, binary correctness) and Langfuse additionally provide integration guidance ( MLflow, 2026 ; Langfuse, 2026 ) . Our study complements Li et al. (2026) with a comparison across 14 decision models and an analysis of query formulation and checklists, reference-guided grading, injection and bias benchmarks, best-of- K K selection, and scaling, base-model and same-size controls. Judge biases and attacks. Position bias ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and length bias ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) in LLM judges are well documented. CALM ( Ye et al., 2024 ) quantifies twelve biases through principle-guided perturbations, and EvalBiasBench ( Park et al., 2024 ) provides hand-written pairs for six bias types. Prompt-injection attacks on judges include optimization-based attacks ( Shi et al., 2024 ) and universal adversarial suffixes ( Raina et al., 2024 ) . Benchmarks. We use JudgeBench ( Tan et al., 2024 ) , LLMBar ( Zeng et al., 2023 ) , the MT-Bench human judgments ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) , RM-Bench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , RewardBench 2 ( Malik et al., 2025 ) , the successor to RewardBench ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , HelpSteer2 ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , PPE ( Frick et al., 2024 ) , EvalBiasBench ( Park et al., 2024 ) and CALM ( Ye et al., 2024 ) . We additionally evaluate long-context judging on LongRewardBench ( Tang et al., 2025 ) and agent-trajectory judging on AgentRewardBench ( Lù et al., 2025 ) . Cascades and calibration. Routing queries between inexpensive and expensive models ( Chen et al., 2023 ) and escalating uncertain judgments with statistical guarantees ( Jung et al., 2024 ) motivate our routing experiments, and we measure calibration with the expected calibration error ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . Appendix B Experimental details B.1 Judges Selection of System-1 models. System-1 models had to expose the typed Noul, Choice and Score interface and be either runnable locally as open weights (up to 9B parameters) or served through the OpenRouter decision-model catalog ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . Selection proceeded in two pre-stated stages (Table 2 ). In the first stage, we took the best available model and a size ladder according to the S1MB English leaderboard ( hotchpotch, 2026 ) : Jev 1.14 (S1MB rank 26 of 205), pplx-decider 1.2 (27B, rank 6) and its 4.5B flash variant (rank 35) ( Perplexity AI, 2026 ) , Clef (27B, rank 38) and Clef-flash (9B, rank 68) ( Cloudflare, 2026 ) , and Kev-4B (rank 104) ( Palmer, 2026 ) . In the second stage, we piloted every other entry of the catalog (30 entries on 2026-10-25, listed by the endpoint’s output_modalities=decisions filter) with 100 JudgeBench calls and included every model that handled our requests reliably and whose projected cost for the full suite was at most $4. Jev 1.14 was served as the generally available release ( typesafe/jev-1.14-20261014 ), whereas S1MB lists the preview release, so its S1MB score may differ slightly from that of the model we evaluated. All models other than Kev were called through OpenRouter with the same System One wire format, questions and inputs as Kev, and calls that still failed after three retries (rate-limit errors for a small number of pplx-flash requests) or that the endpoint rejected as too long are counted as incorrect. Kev-4B as a case study. Kev-4B v1.0 is a LoRA adapter plus pointer head on Qwen3.5-4B-Base ( Palmer, 2026 ; Qwen Team, 2026 ) ; we also run Kev-0.8B and Kev-9B. Its published training mix consists of public classification datasets, generated policy and rule records, consumer-complaint narratives and developer-tooling data, with no human preference data, so every benchmark here is held out for the 0.8B/4B/9B models (the 27B model, which does train on HelpSteer2/3, is not used). All Kev models run locally on an Apple M5 Pro laptop GPU via MLX in bf16 behind the System One API. As a base-model control we serve the untrained Qwen3.5-4B-Base behind the same API, reading next-token probabilities over the same option labels (one prompt format, see Appendix G ). Generative judges. Through an OpenAI-compatible internal gateway (the development deployment for most runs; the PPE 1–100 rerun and the CALM content audit used the production deployment with the same model identifiers after the development key reached its budget): Claude Haiku 5.5 (thinking disabled), GPT-5.6 with reasoning_effort=none , Claude Opus 5.5 with adaptive thinking at medium effort, and GPT-5.6 at medium reasoning effort. As in ( Li et al., 2026 ) , generative judges get the same rubric and must output only a verdict and a probability, with no rationale. Invalid outputs and gateway errors count as wrong (0.74% of Haiku calls, 0.32% GPT-5.6 without reasoning, 0.14% Opus, 0% GPT-5.6 with reasoning). As a same-size generative control, Qwen3.5-4B was additionally evaluated with thinking disabled and with thinking enabled under a 4,000-token budget with budget forcing ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) , served locally on the same hardware (§ E.11 ).
